newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukrainian premier loses grip on power.
newsitem.headline: Ukrainian premier loses grip on power.

text.p: Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, removed from his post on Thursday due to "illness", sees himself as more of a manager than a politician.

It was clear his grip on power was slipping when President Leonid Kuchma appointed First Deputy Prime Minister Vasyl Durdynets acting prime minister "for the time of Pavlo Lazarenko's illness," particularly as Lazarenko's aides said he was feeling fine.
Lazarenko, 44, appointed a year ago as the fifth prime minister of Ukraine since it won independence from Moscow in 1991, comes from a rural family in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
His career began as a driver at a collective farm. Soon, he was the boss and rose to become governor of the region, one of Ukraine's most powerful industrial areas.
Lazarenko, who once described himself as a "manager, not a politician", never spoke publicly on foreign policy issues or on problems in the political life of the country of 51 million.

Described by local mass media in Ukrainian as a "khazyayin" -- boss, or owner -- Lazarenko has devoted his term in office to establishing order in certain, profitable spheres of the economy such as alcohol, tobacco and gas distrubution.

The New York Times published an article recently quoting Western intelligence reports estimating Lazarenko gained about $260 million from unofficial involvement in United Energy Systems, which had a license to import cheap Russian gas.

But Lazarenko denied the charge. "We have corruption in Ukraine as in any other country...Whether I am implicated in all these publications in the mass media, I'm telling you unambigously I am not implicated," he said in Canada last week.

Lazarenko was behind a scheme introduced in 1995 which transferred distribution of imported Russian gas to a dozen private traders. Lazarenko defended the scheme, which, he said, helped slash energy debts to Russia.

Critics of the scheme said traders did not pay all their taxes and that it helped bring about almost $2 billion in unpaid wages. Recently Kuchma and his top aides said it created a monopolistic, uncompetitive energy market.

Lazarenko said he had no ambitions to run in the next presidential elections, due to be held in October 1999, but that he was "young and still had everything in front of him". He also said recently he would back Kuchma if he ran.

Lazarenko once said the ideal system for Ukraine would be a government headed by the leader of the party or group which won parliamentary elections. He is close to several factions in the Verkhovna Rada or parliament.
Lazarenko was linked by local media to so-called "Dnipropetrovsk clan" -- a rival to the "Donetsk clan", also in eastern Ukraine.
The rivalry was highlighted last July when Lazarenko escaped an assassination attempt as his car was blown up on it way to Kiev airport, where he planned to fly to Donetsk.
Later he persuaded Kuchma to sack Donetsk's powerful governor, Volodymyr Shcherban, now leader of the Liberal Party of Ukraine, who was seen then as Lazarenko's personal rival.
Lazarenko speaks German and Russian, and is married with a son and two daughters.
